e) Imperative sentence -> Not a statement.
f) Exclamatory sentence -> Not a statement.

questions.source_solution:

b) Supply is not decreasing.

questions.text:

a) Temperature is increasing (p) and length is expanding (q).
b) Pressure is decreasing (p) or volume is increasing (q).
c) Neither demand is increasing (p) nor price is increasing (q).
d) It is false that Pradeep is bold (p) or Sandeep is handsome (q).
questions.source_solution:

questions.text: Construct truth tables for (a to i):
questions.source_solution:
Truth value results for (TT, TF, FT, FF):
a) (~p) ^ q -> [F, F, T, F]

i) (p <=> q) v (q <=> r) -> [T, T, F, T, T, F, T, T]

b) p v (~q) = T
c) (~p) ^ (~q) = F

e) ~(~p) = T
f) (p v q) ^ (r v s) = T

questions.text:

b) p v q is equivalent to q v p
c) ~[p v (~q)] is equivalent to (~p) ^ q
d) ~[(~p) ^ q] is equivalent to p v (~q)
questions.source_solution:
a) Evaluates to [F, F] -> Contradiction c.
b) Both yield [T, T, T, F] -> Logically equivalent.

b) Truth value: F. Negation: '8 is not prime or 4 is odd.'

questions.text: For the statements (a to c), find antecedent/consequent, converse, inverse, contrapositive, and negation:
questions.source_solution:
a) Ant: 3 is natural; Con: 1/3 is rational. Conv: 1/3 rational => 3 natural. Inv: 3 not natural => 1/3 not rational. Contrap: 1/3 not rational => 3 not natural. Neg: 3 is natural and 1/3 is not rational.
b) Ant: x = 2; Con: x^2 = 4. Conv: x^2 = 4 => x = 2. Inv: x != 2 => x^2 != 4. Contrap: x^2 != 4 => x != 2. Neg: x = 2 and x^2 != 4.
c) Ant: Battery low; Con: Mobile fails. Conv: Mobile fails => battery low. Inv: Battery not low => mobile works. Contrap: Mobile works => battery not low. Neg: Battery low and mobile works.

questions.text: Prove tautologies and contradictions (a to f):
questions.source_solution:
a) p v (~p ^ q) -> [T, T, T, T] (Tautology)
b) (p ^ q) => (p v q) -> [T, T, T, T] (Tautology)
c) ~(p v q) ^ q -> [F, F, F, F] (Contradiction)
d) (p ^ q) ^ ~(p v q) -> [F, F, F, F] (Contradiction)
e) [~q ^ (p => q)] => ~p -> [T, T, T, T] (Tautology)
f) [(p ^ q) => p] => (q ^ ~q) -> [F, F, F, F] (Contradiction)

questions.text:
If A and B are disjoint (A ∩ B = ∅), prove:
a) A ⊆ B'
b) B ∩ A' = B
c) A ∪ B' = B'
questions.source_solution:
a) For any x in A, x is not in B, so x is in B'. Hence A ⊆ B'.
b) B ∩ A' consists of elements in B and not in A = B.
c) Since A ⊆ B', A ∪ B' = B'.

questions.text:
If A ⊆ B, prove:
a) B' ⊆ A'
b) A ∪ B = B
c) A ∩ B = A
questions.source_solution:
a) x in B' implies x not in B implies x not in A, so x in A'. Thus B' ⊆ A'.
b) All elements of A are in B, so A ∪ B = B.
c) Common elements between A and B are A, so A ∩ B = A.

questions.text:
Prove set difference identities:
a) B - A = B ∩ A'
b) A - B = A ∩ B'
c) A - B' = B - A'
questions.source_solution:
a) B - A = {x : x in B and x not in A} = B ∩ A'.
b) A - B = {x : x in A and x not in B} = A ∩ B'.
c) A - B' = A ∩ (B')' = A ∩ B = B ∩ A = B - A'.

questions.text:
If A, B, C are subsets of U, prove distributive laws:
a) A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C)
b) A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)
questions.source_solution:
a) An element x is in A ∪ (B ∩ C) iff x is in A, or (x is in B and x is in C). By logical distribution, this equals (x in A or x in B) and (x in A or x in C), which defines (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).
b) Similarly, x in A ∩ (B ∪ C) means x in A and (x in B or x in C). Distributing gives (x in A and x in B) or (x in A and x in C), defining (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).

questions.text:
Prove De Morgan's laws and set differences:
a) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'
b) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'
c) A - (B ∪ C) = (A - B) ∩ (A - C) = (A - B) - C
d) A - (B ∩ C) = (A - B) ∪ (A - C)
questions.source_solution:
a) x in (A ∪ B)' iff x not in A and x not in B iff x in A' ∩ B'.
b) x in (A ∩ B)' iff x not in A or x not in B iff x in A' ∪ B'.
c) x in A - (B ∪ C) iff x in A and not in B and not in C iff (A - B) ∩ (A - C). Removing B then C gives (A - B) - C.
d) x in A - (B ∩ C) iff x in A and (not in B or not in C) iff (A - B) ∪ (A - C).

b) |x - y| >= |x| - |y|
c) |xy| = |x| * |y|
d) |x/y| = |x| / |y|

questions.text:

a) A ⊆ B'
b) B ∩ A' = B
c) A ∪ B' = B'
questions.source_solution:
Given A ∩ B = ∅:
a) For any x in A, x is not in B, so x is in B'. Hence A ⊆ B'.
b) B ∩ A' consists of elements in B and not in A = B.
c) Since A ⊆ B', taking union with B' yields A ∪ B' = B'.

questions.text:
If A ⊆ B, prove:
a) B' ⊆ A'
b) A ∪ B = B
c) A ∩ B = A
questions.source_solution:
Given A ⊆ B:
a) Let x be in B'. Then x is not in B, which implies x is not in A. Thus x is in A', proving B' ⊆ A'.
b) Since every element of A is already in B, A ∪ B = B.
c) The common elements between A and B are all elements of A, so A ∩ B = A.

questions.text:

a) B - A = B ∩ A'
b) A - B = A ∩ B'
c) A - B' = B - A'
questions.source_solution:
a) B - A = {x : x in B and x not in A} = {x : x in B and x in A'} = B ∩ A'.
b) A - B = {x : x in A and x not in B} = {x : x in A and x in B'} = A ∩ B'.
c) A - B' = A ∩ (B')' = A ∩ B = B ∩ A = B - A'.

questions.text:
If A, B, C are subsets of U, prove distributive laws:
a) A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C)
b) A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)
questions.source_solution:
a) An element x is in A ∪ (B ∩ C) iff x is in A, or (x is in B and x is in C). By logical distribution, this equals (x in A or x in B) and (x in A or x in C), defining (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).
b) Similarly, x in A ∩ (B ∪ C) means x in A and (x in B or x in C). Distributing gives (x in A and x in B) or (x in A and x in C), defining (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).

questions.text:
Prove De Morgan's laws and set differences:
a) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'
b) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'
c) A - (B ∪ C) = (A - B) ∩ (A - C) = (A - B) - C
d) A - (B ∩ C) = (A - B) ∪ (A - C)
questions.source_solution:
a) x in (A ∪ B)' means x is not in (A ∪ B), so x is not in A and x is not in B. Hence x is in A' ∩ B'.
b) x in (A ∩ B)' means x is not in (A ∩ B), so x is not in A or x is not in B. Hence x is in A' ∪ B'.
c) x in A - (B ∪ C) means x is in A and not in B and not in C. Hence (A - B) ∩ (A - C). Removing B then C gives (A - B) - C.
d) x in A - (B ∩ C) means x is in A and not in both B and C. Hence (A - B) ∪ (A - C).

c) Ant: Battery low; Con: Mobile fails. Conv: Mobile fails => battery low. Inv: Battery not low => mobile works. Contrap: Mobile works => battery not low. Neg: Battery low and mobile works.

questions.text: Prove tautologies and contradictions (a to f):
questions.source_solution:
a) p v (~p ^ q) -> [T, T, T, T] (Tautology)
b) (p ^ q) => (p v q) -> [T, T, T, T] (Tautology)
c) ~(p v q) ^ q -> [F, F, F, F] (Contradiction)
d) (p ^ q) ^ ~(p v q) -> [F, F, F, F] (Contradiction)
e) [~q ^ (p => q)] => ~p -> [T, T, T, T] (Tautology)
f) [(p ^ q) => p] => (q ^ ~q) -> [F, F, F, F] (Contradiction)

questions.text:
If A and B are disjoint (A ∩ B = ∅), prove:
a) A ⊆ B'
b) B ∩ A' = B
c) A ∪ B' = B'
questions.source_solution:
Given A ∩ B = ∅:
a) For any x in A, x is not in B, so x is in B'. Hence A ⊆ B'.
b) B ∩ A' consists of elements in B and not in A. Since no element of B is in A, B ∩ A' = B.
c) Since A ⊆ B', taking union with B' yields A ∪ B' = B'.

questions.text:
If A ⊆ B, prove:
a) B' ⊆ A'
b) A ∪ B = B
c) A ∩ B = A
questions.source_solution:
Given A ⊆ B:
a) Let x be in B'. Then x is not in B, which implies x is not in A. Thus x is in A', proving B' ⊆ A'.
b) Since every element of A is already in B, A ∪ B = B.
c) The common elements between A and B are all elements of A, so A ∩ B = A.

questions.text:
Prove set difference identities:
a) B - A = B ∩ A'
b) A - B = A ∩ B'
c) A - B' = B - A'
questions.source_solution:
a) B - A = {x : x in B and x not in A} = {x : x in B and x in A'} = B ∩ A'.
b) A - B = {x : x in A and x not in B} = {x : x in A and x in B'} = A ∩ B'.
c) A - B' = A ∩ (B')' = A ∩ B = B ∩ A = B - A'.

questions.text:
If A, B, C are subsets of U, prove distributive laws:
a) A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C)
b) A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)
questions.source_solution:
a) An element x is in A ∪ (B ∩ C) iff x is in A, or (x is in B and x is in C). By logical distribution, this equals (x in A or x in B) and (x in A or x in C), defining (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).
b) Similarly, x in A ∩ (B ∪ C) means x in A and (x in B or x in C). Distributing gives (x in A and x in B) or (x in A and x in C), defining (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).

questions.text:
Prove De Morgan's laws and set differences:
a) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'
b) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'
c) A - (B ∪ C) = (A - B) ∩ (A - C) = (A - B) - C
d) A - (B ∩ C) = (A - B) ∪ (A - C)
questions.source_solution:
a) x in (A ∪ B)' means x is not in (A ∪ B), so x is not in A and x is not in B. Hence x is in A' ∩ B'.
b) x in (A ∩ B)' means x is not in (A ∩ B), so x is not in A or x is not in B. Hence x is in A' ∪ B'.
c) x in A - (B ∪ C) means x is in A and not in B and not in C. Hence (A - B) ∩ (A - C). Removing B then C gives (A - B) - C.
d) x in A - (B ∩ C) means x is in A and not in both B and C. Hence (A - B) ∪ (A - C).

If A ∩ B = ∅, prove: a) A ⊆ B', b) B ∩ A' = B, c) A ∪ B' = B'
questions.source_solution:
a) x in A implies x not in B, so x in B'. Hence A ⊆ B'.
b) B ∩ A' = {x: x in B and x not in A} = B.
c) A ∪ B' = {x: x not in B or x in B'} = B'.

questions.text: If A ⊆ B, prove: a) B' ⊆ A', b) A ∪ B = B, c) A ∩ B = A
questions.source_solution:
a) x in B' implies x not in B implies x not in A, so x in A'. Thus B' ⊆ A'.
b) Since A ⊆ B, A ∪ B = B.
c) Since A ⊆ B, A ∩ B = A.

questions.text: Prove: a) B - A = B ∩ A', b) A - B = A ∩ B', c) A - B' = B - A'
questions.source_solution:
a) B - A = {x : x in B and x not in A} = B ∩ A'.
b) A - B = {x : x in A and x not in B} = A ∩ B'.
c) A - B' = A ∩ B = B - A'.

questions.text: Distributive laws: a) A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C), b) A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)
questions.source_solution:
a) Follows from logical distribution: x in A or (x in B and x in C) <=> (x in A or x in B) and (x in A or x in C).
b) Follows from: x in A and (x in B or x in C) <=> (x in A and x in B) or (x in A and x in C).

questions.text: De Morgan's Laws: a) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B', b) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B', c) A - (B ∪ C) = (A - B) ∩ (A - C)
questions.source_solution:
a) x in (A ∪ B)' <=> x not in A and x not in B <=> x in A' ∩ B'.
b) x in (A ∩ B)' <=> x not in A or x not in B <=> x in A' ∪ B'.
c) x in A - (B ∪ C) <=> x in A and x not in B and x not in C <=> x in (A - B) ∩ (A - C).
